text: Leadership's vague "know how bad an outage would be" from Lesson 90 is now concrete: no more than 15 minutes of data loss, operational again within one hour. Turn those two numbers into an actual architecture.

Fifteen minutes of acceptable data loss is your RPO. One hour to be operational is your RTO. Naming both before reaching for an architecture is the actual skill — picking a technology first and hoping it fits is working backwards.

An RTO of one hour rules out manual failover — it must be automatic, pointing to Auto-Failover Groups. An RPO of 15 minutes means replication lag is monitored continuously. And a regional disaster means local backups alone aren't enough — you need geo-redundant storage or a cross-region secondary.

Run DBCC CHECKDB on the failed-over copy before calling it recovered. Compare row counts and checksums against the last known-good state. Confirm the app connects through the failover group's listener, not an old server name. Time the whole event to check whether the real numbers held.

Chapter 15's real-world project is complete — Meridian went from one on-prem server with no HA/DR to a migrated, secured, tuned, automated, and disaster-tested Azure environment. Chapter 16, this course's final chapter, is next: exam review, then interview practice.
